spec.description: Small unfilled circle, centre dot and outward radius pointing slightly upward to the right, labelled 4 m. Circumference, radius, centre marker and label use black (#000000); replacing the decorative source-blue circumference is an intentional house-style departure.

The marked segment goes from the centre to the circumference, so it is a radius.

answer.worked:
The base approaches half the circumference, $\frac12(2\pi r)=\pi r$, and the height approaches $r$ as the sectors become thinner.
$$\begin{align*}A &= bh\\A &= \pi r\times r\\A &= \pi r^2\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Two circular plates have radii 12 cm and 13 cm.
Find the difference in their area, correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
For each plate, $A=\pi r^{2}$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{12}&=\pi(12)^{2}\\A_{12}&=144\pi\text{ cm}^{2}\\A_{13}&=\pi(13)^{2}\\A_{13}&=169\pi\text{ cm}^{2}\\A_{\text{difference}}&=169\pi-144\pi\\A_{\text{difference}}&=25\pi\text{ cm}^{2}\\A_{\text{difference}}&\approx78.54\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$$
Rounded to two decimal places.

The area multiplies by $4$.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare circular areas using diameters and explain why adding diameters gives a misleading comparison.

inlines.text: You order a 9-inch pizza from a restaurant.
After a while, the waiter tells you that they no longer have 9-inch pizza bases and will instead give you two 5-inch pizzas instead.
He tries to convince you, saying that you will get more since
Explain to him why this is not a good deal.
pizza sizes are measured according to the diameter.
Round the final area of the 9-inch pizza and the combined area of the two 5-inch pizzas to 2 decimal places.

answer.short: The 9-inch pizza has area $63.62\text{ in}^2$; the two 5-inch pizzas have combined area $39.27\text{ in}^2$. You receive less pizza, so this is not a good deal. Area depends on the square of the radius, rather than the sum of the diameters.
answer.worked:
9-inch pizza: $r=9\div2=4.5\text{ in}$.
$$\begin{align*}A_9&=\pi r^2\\A_9&=\pi(4.5)^2\\A_9&=20.25\pi\text{ in}^2\\A_9&\approx63.62\text{ in}^2\end{align*}$$
Each 5-inch pizza: $r=5\div2=2.5\text{ in}$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{two}}&=2\pi r^2\\A_{\text{two}}&=2\pi(2.5)^2\\A_{\text{two}}&=12.5\pi\text{ in}^2\\A_{\text{two}}&\approx39.27\text{ in}^2\end{align*}$$
Since $12.5\pi<20.25\pi$, the two smaller pizzas provide less pizza. Adding diameters does not compare areas: each area depends on the square of its radius.

answer.worked:
Add the areas of the rectangle and triangle.
$$\begin{align*}
A_{\text{rectangle}} &= 7\times5\\
A_{\text{rectangle}} &= 35\ \text{m}^2\\
A_{\text{triangle}} &= \frac12\times7\times3\\
A_{\text{triangle}} &= 10.5\ \text{m}^2\\
A &= A_{\text{rectangle}}+A_{\text{triangle}}\\
A &= 35+10.5\\
A &= 45.5\ \text{m}^2
\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: $10=\dfrac{50}{360}\times\pi r^2$

answer.worked:
Multiply both sides by $\dfrac{360}{50}$, then divide by $\pi$ and take the positive square root.
$$\begin{align*}10&=\frac{50}{360}\times\pi r^2\\72&=\pi r^2\\\frac{72}{\pi}&=r^2\\\sqrt{\frac{72}{\pi}}&=r\\r&\approx4.8\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$

Multiply both sides by $\dfrac{360}{100}$, then divide by $\pi$ and take the positive square root.
$$\begin{align*}15&=\frac{100}{360}\times\pi r^2\\54&=\pi r^2\\\frac{54}{\pi}&=r^2\\\sqrt{\frac{54}{\pi}}&=r\\r&\approx4.1\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$

If the region between the two circles is divided into six equal segments, what fraction of the area of the outer circle is shaded in the diagram?

spec.description: Two concentric circles with six equal annular sectors. The upper-left, right and lower-left sectors are shaded. The inner disc remains white; no centre marker, dimensions or labels are printed.
spec.mathematics: The outer radius is twice the inner radius. Annular boundaries occur at 30, 90, 150, 210, 270 and 330 degrees. Three of the six annular sectors are shaded.
spec.answerVisibility: The shaded regions are permanent question givens. No supplied answer or solution annotation appears in the diagram.

answer.short: $\frac{3}{8}$. Half the ring is shaded, and the ring occupies $\frac{3}{4}$ of the outer circle.
answer.worked:
Let the inner radius be $r$, so the outer radius is $2r$.
$$\begin{align*}
A_{\text{ring}} &= \pi(2r)^2-\pi r^2 \\
A_{\text{ring}} &= 3\pi r^2
\end{align*}$$
Three of the six equal sectors are shaded, so half the ring is shaded.
$$\begin{align*}
A_{\text{shaded}} &= \frac{1}{2}\times3\pi r^2 \\
\text{Fraction shaded} &= \frac{\frac{3}{2}\pi r^2}{\pi(2r)^2} \\
\text{Fraction shaded} &= \frac{3}{8}
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The shapes in the diagram below have equal areas. Determine the value of $r$.

spec.description: Unshaded circle with its lower-right quadrant removed. Bounding radii point right and down, have matching single ticks, and enclose a right-angle square in the missing quadrant. The downward radius is labelled r.
spec.mathematics: The retained major sector has angle 270 degrees and radius r, so its area is three quarters of pi r squared.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question givens only; no supplied solution is drawn.

spec.description: Unshaded 30-degree minor sector with a horizontal lower radius and an upper radius sloping right. Both radii carry matching double ticks. The lower radius is labelled r + 6.
spec.mathematics: The minor sector has angle 30 degrees and radius r + 6, so its area is one twelfth of pi times (r + 6) squared. Drawing coordinates are construction values, not additional givens.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question givens only; no supplied solution is drawn.

answer.worked:
The left shape is $\frac34$ of a circle; the right shape is $\frac{30}{360}=\frac1{12}$ of a circle.

$$\begin{align*}
\frac34\pi r^2&=\frac1{12}\pi(r+6)^2\\
\frac34 r^2&=\frac1{12}(r+6)^2\\
\frac{r^2}{(r+6)^2}&=\frac19
\end{align*}$$

By trial and error, $r=3$. Checking:

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{3^2}{(3+6)^2}&=\frac9{81}\\
\frac9{81}&=\frac19
\end{align*}$$

Alternate method using quadratic equations:

$$\begin{align*}
\frac34 r^2&=\frac1{12}(r^2+12r+36)\\
-2r^2+3r+9&=0\\
(-2r-3)(r-3)&=0
\end{align*}$$

$r=3$ or $r=-\frac32$, but a radius must be positive. Therefore $r=3$.

entries.description:
You order a 9-inch pizza from a restaurant.
After a while, the waiter tells you that they no longer have 9-inch pizza bases and will instead give you two 5-inch pizzas instead.
He tries to convince you, saying that you will get more since 2 × 5 = 10.
Explain to him why this is not a good deal.
Note: pizza sizes are measured according to the diameter.
entries.expectedAnswer:
9-inch pizza: π(4.5)² ≈ 63.62 in²
2 5-inch pizzas: π(2.5)² × 2 ≈ 39.27 in²
This is not a good deal as two 5-inch pizzas are significantly smaller than a single 9-inch pizza.
(This happens because the radius gets squared; if you halve the radius, the area is a quarter, so giving two pizzas won’t make up the difference.)

presentation.arrangement: Full-width prose prompt with the diameter note immediately beneath it; open working and explanation space below.
presentation.emphasis: Only “Note:” is bold in the diameter note.
presentation.responseSpace: Space for two area calculations and a comparison explanation; dimensions unmeasured.
presentation.suppliedAnswer: Blue calculations and explanation below the prompt; retain in answer fields only.
presentation.teachingContext: Page 4 demonstrates converting diameter to radius before substituting into A = πr² and rounding calculated areas to 2 decimal places.

straightforwardCorrections.text: Round calculated areas to 2 decimal places.
straightforwardCorrections.reason: Makes the precision shown in the supplied answer explicit.

straightforwardCorrections.originalText: (This happens because the radius gets squared; if you halve the radius, the area is a quarter, so giving two pizzas won’t make up the difference.)
straightforwardCorrections.replacementText: Area depends on the square of the radius. Compare the combined areas rather than adding the diameters.
straightforwardCorrections.reason: The halving statement is true generally, but 5 inches is not half of 9 inches; applying it here could mislead students.
